narrative:
The model predicted a 72% chance that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability is well above the acceptance threshold, your law school application was rejected.

The decision was driven primarily by three factors, ranked by importance. Your class rank at the end of your third year was the strongest influence, pushing the prediction strongly toward failure. Placing in the second decile is noticeably lower than the average of roughly sixth-decile performance among students who were admitted. Your first-year class rank was the second most important factor and also pulled the prediction toward failure; you finished in the third decile while admitted students averaged around the sixth.

Your LSAT score was the third most influential piece of information, but it worked in the opposite direction. At 30.5 it sits below the 37.2 average of accepted students, yet the model still treated this score as mildly encouraging relative to the rest of your profile.

Taken together, the model saw your consistently lower class standing in law school as clear evidence that the bar exam would be a significant hurdle. To improve your chances on a future application, focus on raising your academic performance and consider retaking the LSAT to bring that score closer to the level of admitted students. Strengthening those two areas would directly address the factors that most hurt your current prediction.
